title: Due Diligence in Agribusiness, Natural Resource Governance, and Trade: Rethinking Voluntary Standards Under Sustainability Regulations
content:
ABSTRACT

This article examines how sustainability due diligence is reshaping market access, private governance, and natural resource governance in agri-food supply chains. It focuses on the EU Regulation on Deforestation-Free Products (EUDR), which conditions market access on traceability and plot-level geolocation, and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D), which strengthens firm-level obligations to identify and manage environmental and human rights risks across value chains. The study draws on qualitative analysis of WTO Technical Barriers to Trade Committee discussions and 64 interviews with producers, cooperatives, exporters, NGOs, and public officials in Costa Rica's coffee and palm oil sectors. Findings highlight that due diligence requirements reallocate evidentiary responsibilities and associated costs upstream, where participation increasingly depends on digital infrastructure, administrative capacity, and access to finance. Voluntary Sustainability Standards remain relevant as a business-to-business language of sustainability and may continue to provide consumer-facing information, but they are being repositioned as auxiliary tools for risk documentation. The article asserts that sustainability markets are moving toward a new generation of criteria rooted in risk-based traceability, documented environmental and social production conditions, and credible evidence of risk management. These dynamics risk creating “passporting” effects, whereby evidentiary capacity becomes a condition for market participation, with uneven consequences for producers, suppliers, and natural resource governance.
